text:
===== FILE 19950__1.pdf =====
September 2, 2025 
 
 
 
 
The Honorable Douglas Collins 
Secretary  
U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs 
810 Vermont Avenue, NW 
Washington, DC  20420 
 
Re:  RIN 2900-AS31: Reproductive Health Services  
 
Dear Secretary Collins:  
 
On behalf of the physician and medical student members of the American Medical Association 
(AMA), I appreciate the opportunity to offer our comments to the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) on 
the proposal to reinstate the full exclusion of coverage for abortions and abortion counseling for the VA 
medical benefits package and the Civilian Health and Medical Program of the Department of Veterans 
Affairs (CHAMPVA).1 The AMA strongly supports preserving access to evidence-based reproductive 
health care services, including abortion, and supports the basic medical principle that clinical assessments, 
such as the safety of the pregnant patient and appropriate course of treatment, are determinations to be 
made only by physicians with their patients. In alignment with these principles, the AMA asks that the VA 
reconsider its proposed changes to the VA and CHAMPVA reproductive health services benefits and 
retain existing exceptions that permit abortion under certain, limited circumstances. 
 
Under 38 U.S.C. 1710(a)(1) through (3), the VA is authorized to furnish hospital care and medical 
services that the Secretary determines to be needed through the VA’s medical benefits package. Abortion 
care has long been excluded from VA benefits except, prior to 2022, when necessary to preserve the life 
of the pregnant woman. In 2022, the VA revised regulations to permit abortion if the life or health of the 
pregnant beneficiary would be endangered if the pregnancy were carried to term or if the pregnancy was 
the result of rape or incest. The proposed rule would revert coverage to pre-2022 levels to exclude 
abortion and abortion counseling and to permit abortion under CHAMPVA only when a physician 
certifies that the life of the mother would be endangered if the fetus was carried to term. The preamble 
also states that the exclusion of abortion would not apply in life-threatening circumstances under the VA 
benefits package; however, this is not reflected in the proposed revisions to § 17.38. 
 
The shift to allow abortion only when necessary to save the life, but not the health, of the mother is deeply 
concerning and fails to reflect the nature of pregnancy complications. Serious and emergent conditions 
during pregnancy may not be immediately life-threatening but still pose significant risks to patients’ 
health. Conditions such as severe preeclampsia, severe kidney disease, and complications from prelabor 
rupture of membranes can often be resolved, prior to fetal viability, by terminating the pregnancy before a 
patient faces a significant risk of death but, if left untreated, can rapidly become life-threatening with little 
or no warning. Further, there is no bright line in medicine to determine when a condition goes from 
endangering a patient’s health to jeopardizing her life. Reflecting this reality, physicians are trained to 
intervene to prevent the deterioration of a patient’s condition before it becomes life-threatening. But by 
 
1 https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/08/04/2025-14687/reproductive-health-services.  

The Honorable Douglas Collins 
September 2, 2025 
Page 2 
 
 
 
 
eliminating the “health” exception, the proposed rule would tie the hands of physicians caring for veterans 
and their families. Instead of following well-established medical guidelines and medical ethics, physicians 
will be forced to delay appropriate, stabilizing care until the patient’s life is in jeopardy, subjecting 
patients to avoidable risk and needless suffering. We strongly urge the VA to retain the exceptions 
currently recognized in both § 17.38 and § 17.272. 
 
We are also concerned by the proposal to exclude abortion counseling. Counseling is a vital part of the 
informed decision-making process, and the AMA believes that it is essential for physicians to offer clear, 
nonjudgmental, and medically accurate information to their patients, especially when facing difficult and 
personal decisions about abortion. Denying veterans and their families the ability to receive critical 
information about their health and the risks and benefits of different courses of action contradicts 
established medical ethics that prioritize patient autonomy and informed consent. Veterans, like all 
patients, deserve the opportunity to receive unbiased, comprehensive counseling on all their reproductive 
health care options, including, when appropriate, the termination of pregnancy. The removal of counseling 
would severely limit the ability of physicians to support patients in making fully informed decisions about 
their health and their families, and we ask the VA to maintain this coverage.  
 
The termination of pregnancy is a medical matter between the patient and the physician, subject to the 
physician’s clinical judgment, the patient’s informed consent, and the ability to perform the procedure 
safely. Pregnancy complications can develop and worsen quickly, and it is essential that physicians be 
able to exercise their clinical judgment to intervene in accordance with established medical guidelines to 
avert needless suffering and harm. We strongly urge the VA to retain its current coverage of abortion, as 
well as abortion counseling, to ensure that pregnant veterans and their families receive the highest 
standard of care. We greatly appreciate your consideration of our comments and requests. Please reach out 
to me directly at 312-464-5288 or John.Whyte@ama-assn.org if you have questions or need further 
information. 
 
Sincerely, 
 
John Whyte, MD, MPH
